findings.title: Heap buffer overflow via input-controlled copy length in parse_alpha
findings.rationale: Root cause: entry.c:23 assigns claimed from untrusted input with no upper bound, and entry.c:27 passes it directly as the memcpy length into an 8-byte heap allocation. The fix clamps claimed to the allocation size (8) and to the available source bytes (len - 1) immediately after the allocation null-check, before the memcpy.
findings.variants_checked: entry.c:parse_bravo -- uses memcpy(name, buf, len) with the caller-supplied len, not an embedded length field. Different bug class (stack-buffer-overflow), different root cause pattern. Not addressed by this fix. entry.c:parse_charlie -- no memcpy; UAF bug, unrelated pattern.
findings.bypass_considered: An attacker sets buf[0] = 255 (claimed = 255). The first clamp reduces it to 8. The attacker then provides exactly 2 bytes of input (len = 2, so len - 1 = 1). The second clamp reduces claimed to 1. The memcpy writes 1 byte into the 8-byte buffer -- safe.
findings.test_note: No regression test added. The canary target has no C test harness or test directory.
findings.review_reason: The diff is confined to parse_alpha, the only function on the path to the vulnerable memcpy at line 27. It fixes the root cause by clamping claimed to both the allocation size (8) and the available input length (len - 1) before the copy. No new parsing or trust boundaries are introduced. The fix is minimal, idiomatic C, and matches the surrounding literal-constant style.

findings.title: Stack buffer overflow via unbounded memcpy in parse_bravo
findings.rationale: Root cause: entry.c:40 -- memcpy(name, buf, len) copies a caller-controlled length (up to 4095) into a 16-byte stack buffer with no bounds check. The fix clamps len to sizeof(name) - 1 (15) before the copy.
findings.variants_checked: entry.c:parse_alpha -- same unchecked-memcpy pattern (line 27, heap target). Separate finding (f001). entry.c:parse_charlie -- no memcpy, not applicable.
findings.bypass_considered: An attacker supplies exactly 16 bytes of payload (len=15 after the dispatcher subtracts 1). After the clamp, 15 == sizeof(name) - 1, so the condition is false and len stays 15. memcpy writes bytes 0-14, then name[15] is set to '\0'. No overflow.
findings.test_note: No regression test added. The canary target has no C test infrastructure.
findings.review_reason: The single hunk is scoped entirely to parse_bravo, the function containing the bug at entry.c:40. It fixes the root cause by clamping len to sizeof(name) - 1 before the memcpy, preventing the unbounded stack write. No new parsing, trust boundaries, or validation removals are introduced. The idiom is standard C and correctly preserves the existing null-termination at line 41.

findings.title: Heap use-after-free via missing return after conditional free in parse_charlie
findings.rationale: Root cause is entry.c:58 -- free(r) inside the conditional block lacks a return, so execution falls through to entry.c:60 which dereferences the freed pointer. Adding return immediately after free(r) terminates the early-free path before the dangling write.
findings.variants_checked: entry.c:parse_alpha -- single free at function end, no conditional-free-without-return pattern. entry.c:parse_bravo -- stack buffer only, no heap allocation, not applicable.
findings.bypass_considered: An attacker tries buf[0]=0xff to trigger the early-free path. With the fix, that path returns immediately after free(r), so line 60 is never reached. Any other value of buf[0] skips the free entirely, so r is live when line 60 executes.
findings.test_note: No regression test added. The canary target has no C test infrastructure.
findings.review_reason: The single-line return after free(r) at line 58 directly fixes the documented root cause -- a missing early exit that lets execution fall through to the use-after-free write at line 60. The hunk is entirely within parse_charlie. No new parsing, input trust, or validation weakening is introduced. The fix is minimal and matches the early-return idiom already used elsewhere in the file.
